analyst.summary: IRFC is the Railways' financing arm and is about as safe as a lender gets, because it has historically lent to the Ministry of Railways at a government-fixed, wafer-thin markup. But Railways has stopped taking fresh loans from IRFC since FY2023-24, funding new trains and wagons straight from the Union Budget instead. So IRFC's future growth now depends entirely on a newer push into lending to power, renewable-energy, metro and port projects - areas where, for the first time, it carries real repayment risk and competes with older, more experienced government lenders. Profit still grew a healthy 7.8% in FY26 to a record Rs7,009 crore, but that came mostly from wider margins on the new book, not from the underlying business getting bigger - revenue was almost flat. At roughly 2x book value, the market is already paying for this diversification story to succeed smoothly, even though today's return on equity (about 13%) is actually lower than comparable government-owned infrastructure lenders that trade at similar or cheaper valuations. Add a steady drip of government stake sales (the latest 2% offer-for-sale was in June 2026, with more expected) and there isn't enough margin of safety left in the price for a business with a structurally capped lending spread.
